triage.name: Breast Cancer
triage.reason: Palpable breast mass or abnormal screening mammogram is a core case; diagnosis and staging reachable by history, exam, imaging and biopsy.

review_issues: presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: About 1 in 8 US women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in their lifetime; incidence rises steadily with age.
Non-Hispanic White women have the highest overall incidence; Black women are more often diagnosed at a younger age and with more aggressive subtypes, and have higher mortality.
Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry carries a higher rate of BRCA1/BRCA2 founder mutations.
Male breast cancer accounts for under 1% of cases.

risk_factors.text: BRCA1 or BRCA2 pathogenic variant, or other inherited cancer syndrome
Prior breast cancer or prior chest radiation therapy
Prolonged estrogen exposure: early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity or first birth after age 30
Prior benign breast biopsy, especially atypical hyperplasia
Current or recent menopausal hormone therapy with estrogen plus progestin

family_history: Breast cancer in a mother, sister, or daughter
Ovarian cancer in a close relative
Male breast cancer in a relative
Known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation in the family
social_history: Never breastfed or no full-term pregnancy
exposures: Prior therapeutic radiation to the chest (for example, mantle radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma)

chief_complaints.text: I felt a lump in my breast
My mammogram came back abnormal and they want me to have more tests
My nipple has been leaking a little blood
The skin on my breast looks dimpled, like an orange peel

hpi.onset: Gradual; the lump is usually noticed incidentally or on screening imaging, not at a specific moment
hpi.duration: Weeks to months; many patients cannot say exactly when it started
hpi.progression: The lump is typically painless and persists or slowly enlarges; it does not come and go with the menstrual cycle
hpi.location: Most often the upper outer quadrant of the breast; can be anywhere in the breast or axilla
hpi.radiation: Usually none; advanced disease can cause pain radiating to the chest wall, back, or arm
hpi.quality: Firm, hard, irregular, and fixed; may feel like a thickening rather than a distinct ball
hpi.severity: Usually painless; if pain is present it is mild and non-cyclical
hpi.timing: Constant, present every day, not tied to the menstrual period

associated_symptoms.text: A lump or thickening in the armpit
Change in the size or shape of one breast
Skin dimpling or puckering over the lump
Bloody or clear nipple discharge from one breast
Scaly, red, or itchy skin on the nipple and areola
Breast warmth, redness, and swelling with ridged skin
Unintentional weight loss, bone pain, or new shortness of breath suggesting spread

pertinent_negatives: Lump that comes and goes with the menstrual cycle
Redness that started after a piercing or insect bite
Known prior breast cancer treated with lumpectomy at the same site

negatives: Cyclical breast tenderness that resolves after menses
argues_against: Fibrocystic change that fluctuates with the cycle
Mastitis with fever and a recent history of breastfeeding

positives.text: Dimpled or puckered skin over the lump
Scaly, red, or crusted nipple and areola

negatives: Rash that improves with topical antifungal or steroid
argues_against: Eczema of the nipple that responds to topical steroids
Lymphoma presenting with B symptoms and a breast mass

negatives: Mechanical back pain that improves with rest
argues_against: Musculoskeletal strain as the cause of bone pain

negatives: Pleuritic chest pain with a recent viral illness

atypical.how_it_differs: May present only with an abnormal screening mammogram and no palpable lump; tumors can be softer and less distinct on exam, and competing illnesses can delay workup.
missing_classic_features: Breast asymmetry noticed by the patient

atypical.how_it_differs: Presents during lactation or pregnancy with a persistent lump that does not resolve; physiologic breast changes make both self-exam and imaging harder, so diagnosis is often delayed.
missing_classic_features: Clear separation from pregnancy-related breast changes

atypical.how_it_differs: Larger breast size makes self-detection and clinical examination less reliable; patients more often present with a larger tumor or axillary node involvement.

In patients with a history of transplant or prolonged immunosuppression, breast masses may be atypical infections or lymphoproliferative disease rather than carcinoma, so tissue diagnosis is essential.

general.moderate: Well-appearing but anxious; may guard the affected breast
general.severe: Ill-appearing with weight loss or visible skin changes over the breast
general.critical: Toxic-appearing with dyspnea, bone pain limiting movement, or altered mental status from metastatic disease

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants of both breasts with the flat of the fingers, using a systematic pattern
findings.finding: Firm, hard, irregular mass that is fixed to surrounding tissue and does not move freely

findings.maneuver: Inspect the breasts with the patient seated, arms raised, and leaning forward
findings.finding: Dimpling or puckering of the skin overlying the mass (peau d'orange)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nipples and gently press the areola
Gently express the nipple and inspect for discharge
findings.finding: Bloody or clear discharge from a single duct in one breast

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nipple and areola for scaly, red, or crusted skin
findings.finding: Eczematous, scaly, red, or crusted change of the nipple and areola

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the entire breast for warmth, redness, and swelling
findings.finding: Diffuse warmth, erythema, and edema with ridged skin (peau d'orange) without a discrete mass

findings.maneuver: Palpate the axilla with the arm relaxed
findings.finding: Firm, enlarged, or matted axillary lymph nodes

findings.maneuver: Compare the size and shape of both breasts with the patient seated upright
findings.finding: Asymmetry or change in the size or contour of one breast

findings.maneuver: Examine the opposite breast and axilla
findings.finding: No mass, skin change, or lymphadenopathy on the contralateral side

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and assess for systemic signs of infection
findings.finding: No fever or systemic inflammatory signs

findings.maneuver: Ask about and palpate for tenderness that fluctuates with the menstrual cycle
findings.finding: Mass is non-tender and does not change with the cycle

findings.maneuver: Palpate the spine and long bones for focal tenderness
findings.finding: Focal bone tenderness suggesting metastatic disease

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant and percuss the liver span
findings.finding: Hepatomegaly or nodular liver edge suggesting hepatic metastasis

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lung fields and percuss the bases
findings.finding: Decreased breath sounds or dullness at the base suggesting pleural effusion

labs.caveat: Anemia is usually from chronic disease or prior therapy rather than the tumor itself; a low hemoglobin in a patient with bone pain should raise concern for marrow involvement.
An isolated rise can reflect bone metastases or liver involvement; fractionate with GGT if the source is unclear.
Helps confirm that a raised alkaline phosphatase is hepatobiliary rather than bony.
Rises only with significant hepatic replacement or biliary obstruction.
Hypercalcemia suggests osteolytic bone metastases; correct for albumin.
Nonspecific; high values with a rapidly growing mass or liver involvement.
Check before contrast-enhanced staging imaging and before nephrotoxic chemotherapy.
Negative. Required in anyone of childbearing potential before imaging, biopsy, or systemic therapy.

findings.finding: Nonspecific ST-T wave flattening or T-wave inversion

imaging.study: Diagnostic mammography with spot compression and magnification views

findings.text: Fine pleomorphic or linear branching microcalcifications
Architectural distortion without a discrete mass

imaging.preferred_when: Dense breast tissue, palpable mass, or to characterize a mammographic finding

findings.text: Solid hypoechoic mass with irregular or spiculated margins and posterior acoustic shadowing
Taller-than-wide orientation with anti-parallel blood flow on color Doppler
Enlarged, rounded, or cortex-thickened axillary lymph node

imaging.study: MRI breast with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Dense breasts, lobular histology, known BRCA mutation, or to assess extent before breast-conserving surgery

findings.text: Enhancing mass with irregular margins and washout kinetics
Non-mass enhancement in a segmental or linear distribution
Additional ipsilateral or contralateral foci of disease not seen on mammography

imaging.study: CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected metastatic disease or locally advanced tumor

findings.text: Enlarged mediastinal, axillary, or retroperitoneal lymph nodes

imaging.preferred_when: Bone pain or suspected skeletal metastases

findings.text: Focal increased uptake in the spine, ribs, pelvis, or long bones
Diffuse or multifocal uptake suggesting widespread skeletal disease

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected recurrence or equivocal conventional staging

findings.text: Hypermetabolic lymph nodes or distant lesions

initial.test: Diagnostic mammography with spot compression and magnification views
initial.why: First-line characterization of a palpable mass or abnormal screening mammogram
Distinguishes solid from cystic and guides biopsy
initial.only_if: dense breast tissue, palpable mass, or a mammographic finding needing characterization

initial.why: Baseline blood counts before biopsy and any systemic therapy
Baseline renal function, calcium, and electrolytes before contrast imaging and treatment
Rules out pregnancy before imaging, biopsy, and systemic therapy
Baseline hepatic function and screen for hepatic involvement

confirmatory.test: Core needle biopsy of the breast mass
confirmatory.why: Tissue diagnosis with histology, grade, and receptor status (estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, HER2)
Assesses axillary nodal involvement at the time of surgery

supporting.test: MRI breast with and without contrast
supporting.why: Defines extent of disease and screens the contralateral breast
supporting.only_if: dense breasts, lobular histology, known BRCA mutation, or considering breast-conserving surgery

supporting.test: CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.only_if: locally advanced tumor, symptoms suggesting metastasis, or abnormal liver function tests
bone pain or an elevated alkaline phosphatase

supporting.why: Clarifies equivocal findings or suspected recurrence
supporting.only_if: conventional staging is equivocal or recurrence is suspected

supporting.why: Guides surgical and systemic decisions and family screening
supporting.only_if: young age at diagnosis, triple-negative tumor, bilateral disease, male breast cancer, or strong family history

supporting.test: axillary lymph node ultrasound with fine needle aspiration
supporting.why: Confirms nodal involvement when nodes are clinically or radiographically abnormal
supporting.only_if: palpable or suspicious axillary lymph nodes

not_indicated.why: Not a substitute for CT staging; rarely changes management
not_indicated.only_if: respiratory symptoms or an abnormal chest exam

not_indicated.why: Tumor markers are not used to diagnose or stage breast cancer
No role in breast cancer diagnosis or staging
No role in the workup of a breast mass
No role unless infection is suspected
Not part of the breast mass workup
Not indicated for a breast mass
Not part of the diagnostic workup
Not part of the diagnostic workup

decision_points: Any solid breast mass in a woman over 30 is imaged first with diagnostic mammography and ultrasound, then sampled by core needle biopsy rather than excisional biopsy
Pregnancy test before imaging, biopsy, or systemic therapy in anyone of childbearing potential
Receptor status (estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, HER2) on the biopsy specimen drives systemic therapy and must be requested
Axillary ultrasound with fine needle aspiration before sentinel node biopsy when nodes are clinically abnormal
Staging imaging is reserved for locally advanced disease or symptoms; early-stage disease does not need routine CT or bone scan

criteria.name: BI-RADS assessment categories
criteria.summary: A standardized reporting scale for breast imaging: 0 needs additional imaging, 1 negative, 2 benign, 3 probably benign with short-interval follow-up, 4 suspicious and biopsy recommended, 5 highly suggestive of malignancy, 6 known biopsy-proven malignancy. Categories 4 and 5 prompt tissue sampling.

criteria.name: TNM staging for breast cancer
criteria.summary: Stage is assigned from tumor size and chest wall or skin involvement (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M). Stages I through III are non-metastatic and stage IV is metastatic disease.

differential.name: Fibroadenoma
differential.why_considered: Most common benign solid breast mass in young women; presents as a palpable, mobile lump

history: Lump may fluctuate slightly with the menstrual cycle
No weight loss or systemic symptoms
exam: Smooth, well-circumscribed, rubbery, highly mobile mass ('breast mouse')
No skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy
imaging: Oval, well-circumscribed hypoechoic mass with smooth margins on ultrasound

differential.name: Breast cyst
differential.why_considered: Common cause of a palpable breast lump, especially in perimenopausal women

history: May be tender and fluctuate with the menstrual cycle
imaging: Anechoic, round or oval structure with imperceptible walls and posterior acoustic enhancement on ultrasound
Simple cyst resolves or is aspirated; no solid component

differential.name: Fibrocystic breast changes
differential.why_considered: Very common benign condition causing lumpiness and breast pain

history: Bilateral, diffuse lumpiness and cyclical tenderness that worsens before menses and improves after
exam: Diffuse, often bilateral nodularity without a dominant fixed mass
imaging: Diffuse or scattered benign-appearing densities and cysts; no spiculated mass or suspicious calcifications

differential.name: Mastitis or breast abscess
differential.why_considered: Presents with a tender breast mass, redness, and warmth, especially in lactating women

history: Acute onset over hours to days
exam: Warm, erythematous, tender, indurated area; may have fluctuance if abscess
imaging: Ultrasound shows a fluid collection or diffuse inflammatory change; no solid spiculated mass

differential.name: Phyllodes tumor
differential.why_considered: Rare fibroepithelial tumor that can present as a rapidly growing breast mass resembling a fibroadenoma
differential.trigger: A breast mass that grows rapidly or is very large, especially in a younger woman

history: Rapid growth over weeks to months
exam: Large, smooth, mobile mass; skin may be stretched and shiny but not dimpled
imaging: Large, well-circumscribed solid mass with heterogeneous internal echotexture and possible cystic spaces on ultrasound
Mammography shows a large circumscribed mass without spiculated margins

differential.name: Lactational adenoma
differential.why_considered: Palpable breast mass during pregnancy or lactation that can mimic malignancy

exam: Mobile, well-circumscribed mass without skin changes
imaging: Solid, circumscribed mass on ultrasound; biopsy often needed to exclude carcinoma

differential.name: Fat necrosis
differential.why_considered: Can present as a firm, irregular breast mass with skin retraction after trauma or surgery, closely mimicking cancer

history: Recent breast trauma, surgery, or biopsy
exam: Firm, irregular mass that may be fixed; skin dimpling possible
imaging: Coarse, rim-like or 'oil cyst' calcifications on mammography
Ultrasound shows an irregular hypoechoic area; biopsy may be needed if imaging is indeterminate

differential.name: Lymphoma involving the breast
differential.why_considered: Rare but can present as a breast mass, often with systemic B symptoms
differential.trigger: Breast mass with fever, drenching night sweats, or weight loss

history: B symptoms: fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss
imaging: PET/CT shows hypermetabolic breast and nodal disease; biopsy shows lymphoid cells, not carcinoma

differential.name: Metastatic disease to the breast from another primary
differential.why_considered: Rare; another cancer (for example, melanoma, lung, or ovarian) can metastasize to the breast and mimic a primary breast tumor
differential.trigger: Known non-breast malignancy with a new breast mass, or bilateral breast masses

exam: Breast mass without typical primary breast cancer skin changes
Signs of the primary tumor elsewhere
imaging: Imaging features may be atypical; biopsy with immunohistochemistry confirms the origin

severity.mild: Early-stage disease (stage I–IIA): small tumor, no or minimal nodal involvement, no distant spread; patient feels well with a palpable lump or abnormal screening mammogram
severity.moderate: Locally advanced disease (stage IIB–IIIA): larger tumor with skin or chest wall involvement or fixed axillary nodes; may have breast pain, skin changes, or arm swelling
severity.severe: Stage IIIB–IIIC or inflammatory breast cancer: extensive skin involvement, ulceration, matted supraclavicular or internal mammary nodes, or rapidly progressive inflammatory changes
severity.critical: Stage IV metastatic disease with life-threatening complications such as hypercalcemia of malignancy, spinal cord compression, pleural or pericardial effusion, or extensive hepatic replacement

red_flags.finding: Peau d'orange, skin ulceration, or satellite nodules
red_flags.meaning: Locally advanced or inflammatory breast cancer; urgent oncology referral

red_flags.finding: Rapidly enlarging, warm, red, swollen breast
red_flags.meaning: Inflammatory breast cancer; requires urgent biopsy and multidisciplinary care

red_flags.finding: New back pain with focal spinal tenderness or neurologic deficits
red_flags.meaning: Possible spinal cord compression from bone metastasis; emergent imaging and steroids

red_flags.finding: Confusion, polyuria, constipation, or nausea with a high calcium level
red_flags.meaning: Hypercalcemia of malignancy; requires urgent hydration and treatment

red_flags.finding: Shortness of breath with decreased breath sounds or dullness at a lung base
red_flags.meaning: Pleural effusion or pulmonary metastasis; urgent imaging and thoracentesis if large

red_flags.finding: Palpable supraclavicular or fixed matted axillary lymph nodes
red_flags.meaning: Advanced nodal disease; changes staging and treatment approach

complications.name: Lymphedema of the arm
clues: Arm swelling, heaviness, or reduced range of motion

complications.name: Bone metastasis with pathologic fracture or spinal cord compression
Pleural effusion or pulmonary metastasis
clues: Dyspnea, cough, decreased breath sounds at the base

complications.name: Hepatic metastasis with liver dysfunction
clues: Elevated AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, or bilirubin

complications.name: Brain metastasis
clues: Headache, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, altered mental status

complications.name: Local recurrence after breast-conserving surgery
clues: New lump or skin change at the prior lumpectomy site

special_populations.differences: May present only with an abnormal screening mammogram and no palpable lump; tumors can be softer and less distinct; competing comorbidities can delay workup and treatment.

Presents during pregnancy or lactation with a persistent lump that does not resolve; physiologic breast changes make self-exam and imaging harder, so diagnosis is often delayed; staging must avoid ionizing radiation where possible.
Larger breast size makes self-detection and clinical examination less reliable; patients more often present with a larger tumor or axillary node involvement.
Breast masses may be atypical infections or lymphoproliferative disease rather than carcinoma, so tissue diagnosis is essential.

cancer.screening: The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 years. Women at higher risk because of a known BRCA mutation, prior chest radiation, or a strong family history may begin earlier and use MRI in addition to mammography.
cancer.pathology: Most breast cancers are adenocarcinomas arising from the ductal or lobular epithelium. Ductal carcinoma in situ is non-invasive; invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common invasive type. Lobular carcinoma is more often bilateral. Inflammatory breast cancer and Paget disease of the nipple are less common variants. Receptor status (estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, HER2) and grade guide treatment.
cancer.staging_concepts: Staging uses the TNM system: tumor size and chest wall or skin involvement (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M). Stages I through III are non-metastatic; stage IV is metastatic disease. Early-stage disease is often detected by screening before a palpable mass is present.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the lump, and has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months; persistent or slowly enlarging rather than coming and going

key_questions.question: Does the lump change with your menstrual cycle, or is it there all the time?
key_questions.looking_for: Constant and non-cyclical; fluctuation with periods points to benign fibrocystic change

key_questions.question: Is the lump painful?
key_questions.looking_for: Usually painless; mild non-cyclical pain is possible

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any change in the size or shape of that breast?
key_questions.looking_for: Asymmetry or contour change of one breast

key_questions.question: Any dimpling, puckering, or orange-peel appearance of the skin over the lump?
key_questions.looking_for: Skin dimpling or peau d'orange suggesting local invasion

key_questions.question: Has either nipple turned inward or changed in appearance?
key_questions.looking_for: New nipple retraction or scaly, crusted nipple and areola

key_questions.question: Any nipple discharge? If so, from one breast or both, and what color?
key_questions.looking_for: Bloody or clear discharge from a single duct in one breast

key_questions.question: Have you felt any lump or fullness in your armpit or above your collarbone?
Have you had an abnormal mammogram or been told you need more breast imaging?
key_questions.looking_for: Abnormal screening mammogram or BI-RADS 4/5 assessment prompting biopsy

key_questions.question: Have you ever had breast cancer or a benign breast biopsy, especially one showing atypical cells?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior breast cancer or atypical hyperplasia, both raising risk

key_questions.question: Have you ever had radiation therapy to the chest or breast?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior chest radiation, such as mantle radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had breast, ovarian, pancreatic, or prostate cancer, or male breast cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: First-degree relatives with breast or ovarian cancer, male breast cancer, or a known BRCA1/BRCA2 mutation

key_questions.question: How old were you when your periods started, and have you gone through menopause?
key_questions.looking_for: Early menarche or late menopause, meaning longer estrogen exposure

key_questions.question: Have you ever been pregnant, and how old were you at your first full-term birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Nulliparity or first birth after age 30

key_questions.question: Have you used menopausal hormone therapy, and for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or recent combined estrogen plus progestin therapy

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink in a typical week?
key_questions.looking_for: Regular alcohol use, a modifiable risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you had any unintentional weight loss, new back or hip pain, or new shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms suggesting metastatic disease to bone, liver, or lung

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status, which must be known before imaging, biopsy, or systemic therapy

reasoning_points: A persistent, painless, non-cyclical breast mass or an abnormal screening mammogram in a woman over 40
Risk factors such as older age, family history, BRCA1/BRCA2 mutation, prior chest radiation, or prolonged estrogen exposure
Examination findings of a firm, irregular, fixed mass, with or without skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy
Diagnostic mammography and ultrasound showing a spiculated mass or suspicious microcalcifications, followed by core needle biopsy for tissue diagnosis
Receptor status (estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, HER2) requested on the biopsy specimen to guide systemic therapy
Pregnancy excluded before imaging, biopsy, or systemic therapy in anyone of childbearing potential
Staging imaging reserved for locally advanced disease or symptoms suggesting metastasis rather than done routinely in early-stage disease
Benign look-alikes such as fibroadenoma, cyst, fibrocystic change, and mastitis considered and excluded by imaging and, when needed, biopsy

easy: Woman in her 50s or 60s with a painless, firm, fixed breast lump
Classic risk factors such as a first-degree relative with breast cancer
Mammogram shows a spiculated mass with suspicious microcalcifications
medium: Abnormal screening mammogram with no palpable lump in an older adult
Dense breast tissue requiring ultrasound to characterize the finding
Lump with skin dimpling or nipple retraction but no palpable nodes
Woman of reproductive age where fibroadenoma or cyst must be excluded
hard: Inflammatory breast cancer presenting as a warm, red, swollen breast without a discrete mass
Paget disease of the nipple presenting as a scaly, crusted, itchy nipple that fails topical therapy
Pregnancy or lactation with a persistent lump attributed to physiologic breast changes
Metastatic disease presenting first with back pain, hypercalcemia, or shortness of breath
Male breast cancer presenting as a subareolar mass
Lobular carcinoma with subtle imaging findings and bilateral involvement
